paper_title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3Band 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries. 1. Introduction Search-augmented language models tackle knowledgeintensive questions by alternating between chain-of-thought reasoning, issuing search queries, and reading retrieved pas- *Work done during an internship at Tencent. Corresponding author. Figure 1. ECA can credit useful searches in all-failure groups while gating repeated evidence (illustrative example). sages [31]. Recent work has shown that reinforcement learning (RL) with terminal answer rewards can train these multiturn interactions directly in retrieval environments [8, 20, 33] using critic-free group-relative estimators such as GRPO and RLOO [1, 18]. Despite its simplicity, terminal outcome supervision provides coarse signal for multi-step search: single trajectory-level advantage is broadcast uniformly to every generated token. Consequently, well-targeted search that uncovers bridging document is penalized if the model later misstates the final answer, whereas redundant query is reinforced whenever the model answers correctly from parametric memory or an earlier turn. This credit-assignment bottleneck becomes especially acute on hard questions where every sampled rollout in group fails: centered outcome advantages collapse to zero across the group, discarding the gradient even when rollouts retrieved substantially different evidence. Recent methods seek finer-grained supervision by grouping rollouts at repeated environment states [4], scoring retrieved passages against supporting-document annotations 1 [6, 32], or shaping turn-level rewards via changes in the likelihood of the ground-truth answer [23, 28]. When referenceanswer likelihood is evaluated on the full dialogue history, however, the resulting potential reflects not only retrieved documents, but also the agents intermediate reasoning and query phrasing. policy can therefore alter its own potential merely by rewording thought or echoing candidate answers, even when the underlying evidence set has not changed. This motivates central question: can we assign effective step-level credit to search actions using an evidence-only potential that depends strictly on the question and retrieved documents? To address this question, we propose Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA). During training, frozen snapshot of the current policy teacher-forces canonical reference answer under dedicated scoring prompt containing only the question and the deduplicated documents consumed up to each search slot. Stripping generated thoughts and search queries from the scoring context makes the potential Φ(D) invariant to surface reasoning variations: search action changes the potential if and only if it introduces new documents that shift the likelihood of the reference answer. This readout requires no gold passage labels, separate process reward models, or rollout continuations, and is discarded entirely at test time. Within the ECA framework, we study how step-wise potential changes should be aggregated and normalized into token-level advantages. We compare two return constructions: ECA-Step, which clips single-step potential increments before accumulating future progress, and ECAHorizon, which preserves the unclipped telescoping difference between the terminal horizon potential and the potential prior to search. Both variants standardize returns via crossfold normalization (so trajectorys own evidence gain does not inflate its normalization baseline) and apply novelty gate that withholds positive suffix credit when query returns no new document IDs. Crucially, the resulting auxiliary advantage is added to the full search action (both the search call and its preceding reasoning tokens), leaving final-answer tokens under pure outcome supervision. We evaluate ECA across seven Search QA benchmarks totaling 51,713 test questions with Qwen2.5-3Band 7BInstruct [29], and test zero-shot transfer to MultiHop-RAG [21]. Our main contributions are: We formulate an evidence-only answer potential and bounded search-local advantage for outcome-supervised RL, restoring informative credit in over 97% of all-failure rollout groups without passage annotations or external reward models. We analyze how step-wise increment clipping interacts with multi-step evidence accumulation, comparing stepclipped returns (ECA-Step) and horizon-level telescoping returns (ECA-Horizon) alongside ablations on token placement and cross-fold normalization. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over our matched GRPO baseline by +1.03 percentage points (pp) at 3B and +4.80 pp at 7B, outperforming RLOO and GiGPO at both scales while achieving strong zero-shot transfer on MultiHopRAG inference questions. 2. Related Work Credit assignment for multi-turn agents. Assigning steplevel credit from sparse outcomes is central challenge in RL for reasoning and tool-use agents. Process reward models supervise intermediate steps using human or automated annotations [14, 26], whereas VinePPO estimates step values via Monte Carlo rollout continuations [10], and recent multi-turn formulations separate terminal, delayed, and per-turn rewards to reduce variance across long horizons [12, 27]. For retrieval agents, several works derive intermediate signals from corpus annotations: StepSearch rewards gold-document coverage while penalizing redundant queries [32], PiCA trains reward model from pivot annotations [15], and related methods ground credit in annotated retrieval dependencies [6] or counterfactual query verification [7]. Without passage annotations, IGPO [23] and TIPS [28] shape turn-level rewards using changes in reference-answer likelihood across the dialogue prefix, with IGPO normalizing immediate length-scaled log-likelihood gains before discounted accumulation. ECA builds on this likelihood-based paradigm, but restricts the scoring prompt strictly to the question and deduplicated retrieved documents (excluding generated thoughts and queries) and studies stepclipped versus horizon-level returns under search-local credit assignment. Group-relative policy optimization. Critic-free estimators such as GRPO and RLOO compute relative advantages across multiple rollouts per prompt [1, 18], paradigm widely adopted in outcome-supervised search agents including Search-R1, ReSearch, and R1-Searcher [2, 8, 19]. Because trajectory-level normalization assigns one scalar to all turns and collapses when all rollouts fail, recent extensions refine the comparison group or reweight round contributions: GiGPO groups actions at identical or similar intermediate states [4], KnowGPO clusters rollouts by LLM-verified atomic knowledge conditions [3], and CW-GRPO uses an LLM judge to reallocate outcome advantages across rounds [24]. Rather than requiring state collisions, external LLM verifiers, or successful donor trajectories, ECA retains the group-normalized terminal advantage and adds bounded search-local residual standardized via cross-fold normalization within each questions rollout group (see Appendix for detailed comparison). 2 3. Experimental Setup Models and training protocol. We conduct experiments on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. All RL methods are trained on an 8,192-question pool (4,096 from Natural Questions and 4,096 from HotpotQA), with an independent 1,024-question in-domain development set. Training runs for 256 optimizer updates with learning rate 106, 5 sampling 32 questions with = 8 rollouts per question at each update (256 trajectories per step; 65,536 total). Forward passes use BF16 mixed precision with FP32 master weights and AdamW states (with CPU optimizer offloading at 7B). Search environment. Within each episode, the agent can take up to four actions (at most = 3 search calls followed by final answer), generating up to 512 tokens per action within 4,096-token context window. Rollouts are sampled at temperature 1.0 during training and decoded greedily at evaluation. Retrieval is served by frozen E5-base-v2 retriever [25] over Wikipedia18, returning the top-3 passages per query via exact FP32 inner-product search. Malformed or unfinished episodes are retained in evaluation and scored as incorrect if they fail to produce matching answer. Baselines and checkpoint selection. We compare ECAStep and ECA-Horizon against three RL baselines reproduced under the same 8,192-question training pool and 65,536-trajectory budget: (i) GRPO (λ = 0 in Eq. 8), (ii) RLOO [1], and (iii) GiGPO (w/std) [4], alongside the untrained Base agent. We also report published results for R1-Instruct, Search-R1, ZeroSearch, and StepSearch from Feng et al. [4], and TIPS from Xie et al. [28]. Checkpoints are evaluated every 32 updates on the 1,024-question development set (breaking ties toward earlier steps), and the single best development checkpoint per run is used across all test suites and transfer evaluations. Both ECA variants use λ = 0.1, selected on the development set for ECA-Step and transferred directly to ECA-Horizon without retuning (Appendix B). Evaluation benchmarks and metrics. Following SearchR1 and GiGPO [4, 8], we evaluate on seven QA benchmarks totaling 51,713 test questions: two in-domain datasets (NQ, HotpotQA) and five out-of-domain datasets (TriviaQA, PopQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle). Our primary metric is strict question-level Exact Match (EM). For question q, let eq = 1 if the normalized nonempty prediction matches any normalized ground-truth alias (after lowercasing and stripping punctuation, articles, and extra whitespace), and eq = 0 otherwise. We report the unweighted macro-average across the seven datasets: EM = 100 7 1 s=1 (cid:88) qQs (cid:88) eq, (10) where is the test set of benchmark (Appendix B.3). Zero-shot transfer to MultiHop-RAG. To test whether learned search behaviors generalize to new corpus and longer documents without further tuning, we evaluate the selected Search QA checkpoints zero-shot on MultiHopRAG [21]. The agent retrieves top-3 chunks (using E5-basev2 and up to three searches within 16,384-token context) over 6,532 chunks segmented from 609 news articles. We report performance on the 816 multi-hop inference questions following the TreeHop protocol [13]. 5. Results and Analysis 5.1. Main Results on Search QA Table 1 presents strict question-level EM across the seven Search QA benchmarks. Starting from the untrained Base agents (21.75 macro EM at 3B and 29.93 at 7B), outcomesupervised RL substantially improves multi-turn retrieval and answering, with GRPO reaching 37.19 (3B) and 37.82 (7B). Augmenting terminal outcome supervision with our evidence-only credit signal yields consistent further gains across both model scales. At 3B, ECA-Step and ECAHorizon reach 38.05 and 38.22 macro EM, outperforming GRPO by +0.86 and +1.03 percentage points (pp) and improving over the Base agent by +16.29 and +16.46 pp, respectively. At 7B, the advantage of evidence-based credit is even more pronounced: ECA-Step reaches 41.65 EM (+3.83 pp over GRPO) and ECA-Horizon achieves 42.62 EM, surpassing GRPO by +4.80 pp, RLOO (40.56) by +2.06 pp, and the Base agent by +12.69 pp. ECA-Horizon also outperforms the state-grouped GiGPO (w/std) baseline at both scales (38.22 vs. 36.96 at 3B, +1.26 pp; 42.62 vs. 41.09 at 7B, +1.53 pp). Compared against published likelihood-shaping and search RL baselines, ECAHorizon exceeds TIPS (33.60 at 3B and 41.71 at 7B [28]) by +4.62 and +0.91 pp and Search-R1 (32.5 and 38.5) by +5.72 and +4.12 pp. Examining individual benchmarks reveals two notable trends. First, the benefit of ECA scales strongly with model capacity: moving from 3B to 7B widens ECA-Horizons margin over GRPO from +1.03 pp to +4.80 pp, with large gains on HotpotQA (+4.09 pp), Bamboogle (+8.00 pp), and NQ (+5.57 pp). Because ECA uses the policy itself as the frozen scorer Φi(D), stronger 7B backbone provides sharper answer-likelihood estimates while avoiding GRPOs early plateau on multi-hop retrieval. Second, preserving horizon-level gains (ECA-Horizon) outperforms step-wise clipping (ECA-Step) on aggregate EM at both scales, especially on 7B 2WikiMultiHopQA (39.35 vs. 35.95) and Bamboogle (40.00 vs. 37.60), while ECA-Step remains competitive on splits such as 7B MuSiQue (17.75 vs. 16.88). 5.2. Ablations on Credit Assignment Design Table 2 isolates the core design choices of ECA at 3B (λ = 0.1). First, where auxiliary credit is applied along the trajectory is critical. Restricting ECA-Steps credit mask to the <search> query tokens alone (excluding the preceding <think> tokens) causes macro EM to drop from 38.05 to 35.27, falling below outcome-only GRPO (37.19). Conversely, broadcasting the first-slot evidence advantage across all trajectory tokens (without local novelty gating) reaches only 36.42 EM. Deciding what to query happens during the reasoning tokens preceding the search call: supervising only the query tag decouples search planning from query execution, whereas trajectory-wide broadcasting blurs turn-level attribution and leaks search credit into the final answer step. Second, comparing return constructions at 3B, both ECA-Step (38.05 EM, 46.76 F1) and ECA-Horizon (38.22 EM, 45.80 F1) substantially outperform outcome-only GRPO (37.19 EM) as well as the query-only (35.27 EM) and broadcast (36.42 EM) ablations (see Appendix for the analysis of cross-fold vs. full-group normalization). Between the two variants, ECA-Step attains slightly higher token F1 at 3B, whereas ECA-Horizon achieves higher strict EM at both 3B (+0.17 pp) and 7B (+0.97 pp), confirming that preserving unclipped horizon gains becomes increasingly beneficial as model capacity scales. 5.3. On paired per-question basis against the Base agent, ECA-Horizon converts 12, 340 previously wrong answers to correct at 3B (vs. 2, 166 regressions) and 8, 861 to correct at 7B (vs. 2, 158 regressions). 5.4. Zero-Shot Transfer to MultiHop-RAG Table 3 reports zero-shot transfer to the 816 multi-hop inference questions of MultiHop-RAG [13, 21]. On these compositional inference queries, where the agent must synthesize facts across multiple news articles, both ECA variants outperform all baselines: at 3B, ECA-Step reaches 84.68 EM (+4.66 pp over GRPOs 80.02 and +1.22 pp over RLOOs 83.46), while at 7B, ECA-Horizon reaches 89.22 EM (+6.38 pp over GRPOs 82.84, +1.97 pp over GiGPOs 87.25, and +1.11 pp over RLOOs 88.11). 8 6. Conclusion We presented Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), training-only credit assignment framework for searchaugmented language models. By evaluating the loglikelihood of canonical reference answer under an evidenceonly prompt containing solely the question and deduplicated retrieved documents, ECA isolates the informational contribution of each search action from surface variations in intermediate reasoning and query phrasing. Comparing stepclipped increments (ECA-Step) against telescoping horizon potential differences (ECA-Horizon) within shared training pipeline, we showed that ECA-Horizon consistently improves strict macro exact match over outcome-only GRPO, RLOO, and state-grouped GiGPO across seven Search QA benchmarks at both 3B and 7B scales, and transfers effectively zero-shot to MultiHop-RAG multi-hop inference queries.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Several limitations of our study point to directions for future work. First, our current empirical evaluation focuses on the search-augmented question answering domain and has not yet been extended to broader multi-turn agent settings such as code generation, interactive debugging, or general tooluse environments. Adapting evidence-only credit assignment to these broader agent domains (where intermediate observations take the form of execution traces, compiler diagnostics, or structured API responses) is an important direction for future work. In addition, computing Φi(D) introduces batched teacher-forced forward passes during training, although testtime inference cost remains unchanged. Second, reference-answer log-likelihood under single canonical alias is an imperfect proxy for document utility: passage may provide an intermediate bridge entity without immediately raising the probability of final answer tokens, and document-ID deduplication does not detect near-duplicate text across different articles.
